title: Smart Pointers: unique_ptr and shared_ptr
learningObjectives: Explain unique_ptr exclusive and shared_ptr shared ownership.
Use weak_ptr to observe without extending lifetime.

understand.concept: unique_ptr represents exclusive ownership; shared_ptr represents shared ownership using a reference count. Use make_unique/make_shared and avoid shared ownership unless needed.
understand.whyItMatters: Smart pointers encode ownership and reduce manual cleanup mistakes.
understand.explain: Do not copy unique_ptr; avoid cycles with shared_ptr; use weak_ptr for non-owning links in cycles.

examples.title: Exclusive owner
examples.explanation: unique_ptr owns the object and cleans it up automatically.

examples.title: Observe without owning
examples.explanation: weak_ptr does not extend lifetime; it can check whether owner remains.

examples.title: Prefer ownership types
examples.explanation: Container holds unique owners; objects are automatically cleaned up.

practise.guidedTask: For Smart Pointers: unique_ptr and shared_ptr, draw the object and pointer/reference relationships for every example. Mark owner, target, constness, lifetime, validity of access, and any operation that could invalidate the pointer or reference.
practise.independentTask: Write a focused C++ exercise for Smart Pointers: unique_ptr and shared_ptr. Demonstrate at least three cases, including a safe usage and a boundary/invalid case explained in comments but not executed. State who owns the resource and when each object/view is valid.
hints: Draw the pointer/reference and its target object.
Mark whether the object is alive and who owns it.
Check nullptr and bounds before access.
Consider invalidation, deletion and scope exit.
Use standard containers or smart pointers when they express ownership more safely.

questions.explanation: weak_ptr does not keep object alive.
